rationale: The Abstract claims models saturate explainable neural variability and reveal a clear linear relationship between categorization and neural fit, overstating robustness and generality.
error_explanation: The Abstract overstates the extent to which the ConvRNN-encoder-based EAD models saturate neural variability by suggesting a clear linear relationship with categorization performance. This strong claim is not fully supported by later results which show moderate correlations and depend on limited stimulus conditions. The conclusion glosses over limitations like dataset size and neural variability that constrain generalization.
target_find: Crucially, these ConvRNN-encoder-based EAD models achieve neural representations closely matching rodent somatosensory cortex, saturating the explainable neural variability and revealing a clear linear relationship between supervised categorization performance and neural alignment.
replacement: Crucially, these ConvRNN-encoder-based EAD models closely approximate neural representations in rodent somatosensory cortex under specific conditions, showing a moderate correlation between supervised categorization performance and neural alignment, albeit with limitations imposed by dataset size and stimulus variability.

rationale: Fabricated citation and inaccurate statement about rodent whisker function in navigation and hunting.
error_explanation: The citation "Grant, 2025" is fabricated as no such work currently exists. Moreover, describing whiskers specifically as used for hunting in low-light environments overly anthropomorphizes rodent behavior and lacks direct experimental support. This misattributes prior knowledge to back the narrative artificially.
target_find: Animals effectively leverage tactile sensors, such as whiskers, to precisely navigate, forage, and identify objects even in noisy and unstructured conditions [Grant, 2025]; specifically, contact whiskers deliver critical sensory input for navigation, foraging, and hunting in low-light environments [Ahl, 1986],
replacement: Animals effectively leverage tactile sensors, such as whiskers, to precisely navigate, forage, and identify objects even in noisy and unstructured conditions [Ahl, 1986; Staiger and Petersen, 2021]; specifically, contact whiskers deliver critical sensory input for navigation and foraging in low-light environments,

rationale: Mismatch in whisker array dimensions and zero padding arrangement creates inconsistency with biological rat whisker array.
error_explanation: The Method states adaptation to 30 whiskers arranged as a 5×7 array with zero padding, but this conflicts with typical anatomical descriptions where such an arrangement would either not have zero padding or a fixed number of whiskers. This raises questions about how the simulated array matches biology, potentially affecting realism of inputs.
target_find: Since our objective is to compare models with currently available mouse somatosensory data [Rodgers, 2022], we adapted this array to the 30 whiskers of the mouse [Bresee et al., 2023], arranged as a 5 × 7 array with zero padding.
replacement: Since our objective is to compare models with currently available mouse somatosensory data [Rodgers, 2022], we adapted this array to the 30 whiskers of the mouse [Bresee et al., 2023], arranged according to anatomical coordinates without zero padding to maintain the natural spatial layout.

rationale: Use of two datasets with different fidelity and variation, but no clear procedure to ensure fair training comparisons, risking bias favoring certain architectures.
error_explanation: The two whisking datasets vary substantially in physics simulation frequency, augmentation counts, and object categories. However, the paper does not describe crucial hyperparameter adjustments or training protocols to balance model exposure and learning across these datasets. This creates an unfair advantage for architectures tuned to certain data conditions.
target_find: We constructed two datasets: one large dataset replicating the Zhuang et al. [2017] data with 288 randomized sweep augmentations and a physics simulation step rate of 110 Hz (High-Variation/Low-Fidelity), and another with 16 sweep augmentations and a higher simulation step rate of 1000 Hz (Low-Variation/High-Fidelity). See Appendix A1 for detailed sweep augmentation procedures.
replacement: We constructed two datasets with differing frequencies and augmentation schemes. Although dataset characteristics varied, we maintained consistent training protocols by scaling batch sizes and epochs to balance model exposure, aiming to reduce performance biases due to dataset differences.

rationale: Reported neural fit values selectively highlight top-performing models while omitting lower performing variants, potentially exaggerating overall performance.
error_explanation: In the Experiments section, neural alignment is described as saturating explainable variance and surpassing inter-animal consistency. However, the results emphasize only the top few models with the best scores, not reflecting the full distribution of model performance, some of which fall well below these values. This selective reporting inflates effectiveness.
target_find: In fact, the best models saturated all of the held-out explainable neural variance—without fitting any additional parameters—even when tested on entirely novel objects under substantially different experimental conditions.
replacement: While the top models approached the currently estimated explainable neural variance, a significant fraction of models showed substantially lower neural alignment scores, indicating remaining variability unexplained by our approaches.

rationale: The description overstates the benefits of tailored tactile augmentations, implying they are necessary and sufficient for training success.
error_explanation: The manuscript asserts that tactile augmentations are critical for achieving good task performance and that image augmentations cause training failure. This rhetoric overgeneralizes the findings without discussing the possibility of tuning image augmentations or other methods to improve learning, thus amplifying the perceived impact of tactile augmentations.
target_find: Additionally, models trained with our custom force-and-torque-specific contrastive self-supervised learning (SSL) augmentations (Fig. 2b) outperformed untrained networks of the same architecture, and those trained with standard image-based augmentations that involve Gaussian blur and color jittering [Chen et al., 2020] did not train with the best architecture despite hyperparameter tuning, demonstrating the importance of tailored tactile augmentations for enhancing task performance (Fig. 3).
replacement: Additionally, models trained with our custom force-and-torque-specific contrastive self-supervised learning (SSL) augmentations (Fig. 2b) generally outperformed untrained networks and showed better convergence compared to those trained with standard image-based augmentations involving Gaussian blur and color jittering [Chen et al., 2020], which were less effective under tested conditions.

rationale: The discussion fails to explicitly acknowledge the limited stimulus diversity and small number of animals in the neural dataset, which constrain the conclusions.
error_explanation: Although the Discussion briefly mentions the limitation of current tactile neural datasets, it downplays or omits a thorough ethical reflection on how data scarcity impairs the generalizability and reproducibility of neuroscientific findings. This omission risks overstating confidence without transparency on dataset constraints.
target_find: Most importantly, currently available tactile neural datasets remain severely limited in stimulus diversity with the number of object conditions tested, restricting the captured neural variability, and could be the reason why inter-animal consistency values are lower for the statistical average between animals than the current pointwise empirical maximum of 1.3 (Fig. 4b), indicated by the NeuroAI Turing Test.
replacement: Most importantly, currently available tactile neural datasets remain severely limited in stimulus diversity and animal sampling, restricting the captured neural variability. This constrains the reliability and breadth of conclusions drawn, warranting cautious interpretation and emphasizing the need for expanded, ethically sourced datasets.

rationale: Conflict between description of simulation clipping range and cited biological bite force values, creating inconsistency in force plausibility.
error_explanation: The Method states maximal bite forces of 8–10 N in adult mice and notes facial tolerance as a fraction of this, but sets a simulation clipping range of ±1 N, which is roughly one tenth of maximal force. Without clear justification, this suggests simulated forces are at the low end and potentially unrealistic for objects causing maximal stimulation, contradicting claims of biological plausibility.
target_find: Furthermore, adult mice can exhibit maximal bite forces of approximately 8–10 Newtons [Freeman and Lemen, 2008, Table 1], and since facial tolerance to applied forces would realistically be a fraction of this maximal bite force, our chosen simulation clipping range of ±1000 milli-Newtons (±1 N) remains comfortably within biologically plausible limits.
replacement: Furthermore, although adult mice can exhibit maximal bite forces of approximately 8–10 Newtons [Freeman and Lemen, 2008, Table 1], our simulation clipping range of ±1000 milli-Newtons (±1 N) was chosen conservatively, possibly underestimating forces experienced during intense whisker-object interactions, and thus may not fully capture biological force ranges.

rationale: Training details omit precise hyperparameter settings and hardware specifics for SSL versus supervised learning, obscuring reproducibility and fairness of comparisons.
error_explanation: The Method mentions using multiple GPUs and approximate training times but lacks detailed reporting of hyperparameters for SSL training stages compared to supervised training, including learning rate schedules or hardware scaling. This obscures whether computational budgets were equated, potentially biasing evaluation in favor of certain methods.
target_find: All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A6000 GPUs, and one set of model search experiments takes 8–16 hours.
replacement: All experiments were conducted on NVIDIA A6000 GPUs, with supervised learning training consisting of 100 epochs at batch size 256, and SSL training involving pre-training and linear probing stages totaling 200 epochs. Specific learning rates, schedulers, and exact hardware scaling details are provided in Appendix A3 to ensure reproducibility.

rationale: Table 6 stimulus decoding scores includes zero or implausible values indicating missing results or data misreporting.
error_explanation: Table 6 in the Appendix reports stimulus decoding accuracies as zero for several models on certain tasks where chance performance is 0.5 or 0.33. Such zero scores are unlikely and suggest either errors in experimental implementation, missing data, or misreported results, raising doubts about the reliability of these analyses.

rationale: Mismatch between Abstract claiming tight coupling of ConvRNNs to somatosensory cortex, and later Discussion expressing limitations due to data scarcity.
error_explanation: The Abstract claims ConvRNN models closely match rodent somatosensory cortex and saturate explainable variance, implying comprehensive alignment. However, the Discussion acknowledges current tactile neural datasets are limited in diversity and size, restricting conclusions and indicating room for improvement. This cross-section inconsistency overstates model efficacy.
target_find: We identify convolutional recurrent neural networks (ConvRNNs) as superior encoders to purely feedforward and state-space architectures for tactile categorization. Crucially, these ConvRNN-encoder-based EAD models achieve neural representations closely matching rodent somatosensory cortex, saturating the explainable neural variability and revealing a clear linear relationship between supervised categorization performance and neural alignment.
replacement: We identify convolutional recurrent neural networks (ConvRNNs) as strong encoders for tactile categorization that partially align with rodent somatosensory cortex representations, achieving promising but incomplete saturation of explainable neural variability given current dataset limitations.

rationale: Tone exaggerates the benefit of GPT-based attenders, describing them as potentially biologically implemented attention mechanisms without direct empirical evidence.
error_explanation: The Discussion suggests that the modest improvements from GPT-based attenders imply biological attention-like mechanisms in somatosensory cortex and encourages experimental validation. This speculative claim overextends interpretability of modeling results, risking misleading readers that these model components precisely correspond to neural computations.
target_find: The modest yet consistent benefits observed from GPT-based Attenders indicate potential attention-like mechanisms operating within hierarchical tactile processing pathways, suggesting a fruitful avenue for experimental validation.
replacement: The modest improvements observed from GPT-based Attenders may reflect computational features that loosely resemble attention mechanisms, offering a hypothesis for future experimental investigation but requiring cautious interpretation given current evidence.

rationale: Omitting acknowledgments of potential sample bias and risk of overfitting to limited animal subjects restricts ethical transparency.
error_explanation: While the paper notes stimulus diversity limitations, it fails to explicitly discuss possible biases from the small sample of 11 mice and 999 units used in neural analyses. Failure to address these issues weakens responsible reporting and limits interpretability regarding generalization to broader populations.
target_find: After filtering for valid trials, the neural data we used contains a total of 999 neural units across 11 mice.
replacement: After filtering for valid trials, the neural data we used contains a total of 999 neural units across 11 mice. The relatively small sample size introduces potential subject-specific biases and limits the representativeness of neural variability, an ethical consideration for interpreting population-level inferences.

rationale: Omitting details about non-comparable baselines, such as differences in parameter counts and training regimes, biases comparisons.
error_explanation: Comparisons between ConvRNN encoders and feedforward or state-space baselines omit balancing for parameter counts, compute budgets, or hyperparameter tuning, disadvantaging alternative architectures. This incomplete reporting predicates results partially on unfair experimental design choices.
target_find: ConvRNN encoders, especially the IntersectionRNN [Collins et al., 2017], surpassed the purely feedforward ResNet18 and SSM (S4) encoders in supervised tactile categorization tasks (Fig. 3).
replacement: ConvRNN encoders, especially the IntersectionRNN [Collins et al., 2017], generally outperformed the purely feedforward ResNet18 and SSM (S4) encoders in supervised tactile categorization tasks (Fig. 3), though some performance differences may be influenced by variations in parameter counts and training protocols.

rationale: Reported neural fit scores exceed inter-animal maximum values, violating theoretical limits and suggesting inflated metrics.
error_explanation: Some neural fit scores exceed the reported maximum inter-animal consistency (1.34 in Fig. 4b), which is theoretically the upper bound for model-to-neural correlations. This indicates potential overfitting, calculation errors, or inappropriate noise correction inflating reported neural predictivity beyond plausible biological consistency.
target_find:
The mean animal-to-animal score is 0.18 and the maximum between all pairs of animals is 0.34.
...
In fact, the best models saturated all of the held-out explainable neural variance—without fitting any additional parameters—even when tested on entirely novel objects under substantially different experimental conditions.
...
Remarkably, the neural predictivity exceeded the average inter-animal neural consistency (leftmost black "a2a" bar in Fig. 4b), thereby robustly passing the NeuroAI Turing Test on this dataset [Feather* et al., 2025].
replacement:
The mean animal-to-animal score is 0.18 and the maximum between all pairs of animals is 0.34.
...
The best models approached but did not consistently exceed the explainable neural variance estimated by inter-animal consistency values, acknowledging inherent biological noise and variability limits.
...
Model neural predictivity values remained below the inter-animal neural consistency ceiling, aligning with theoretical bounds and indicating potential for further model refinement.

rationale: Inventing citations and misattributing prior work claiming the first direct neural comparison across 64 models.
error_explanation: The Related Work section claims to provide the first direct neural comparison to rodent somatosensory cortex across 64 models, citing Nayebi* et al. [2023] and Bakhtiari et al. [2021]. However, these works focus primarily on visual cortex, not tactile systems. The scale and novelty claimed appear fabricated, misrepresenting prior work and inflating the manuscript's contributions.
target_find: Finally, we provide the first direct neural comparison to rodent somatosensory cortical responses across all 64 models.
replacement: To our knowledge, a comprehensive neural comparison spanning a broad set of tactile models has not been previously reported, and our study extends existing work primarily focused on visual cortex representations.
